questions.question: Q: What is the 'male gaze' and how does it operate in media products?
questions.correctAnswer: The male gaze (Mulvey, 1975) argues that mainstream media positions the audience to view women through a heterosexual male lens, objectifying their bodies for visual pleasure. The camera lingers on women's bodies, and female characters are often defined by their appearance rather than their actions or personality. Audiences of any gender are positioned to identify with this male viewpoint.

questions.question: Q: How have representations of masculinity changed in contemporary media?
questions.correctAnswer: Traditional hyper-masculinity (strong, silent, aggressive) is still common in action films and games, but the 'new man' representation shows men as emotionally expressive, nurturing, and domestically competent. Advertising increasingly uses this representation. However, toxic masculinity persists in some media, reinforcing harmful expectations about male behaviour.

questions.question: Q: Evaluate whether media representations of gender are improving.
questions.correctAnswer: Improvements are evident: more female protagonists, stronger Bechdel Test results, the 'new man' representation, and growing LGBTQ+ visibility. Streaming platforms commission diverse content. However, progress is uneven — the male gaze persists in music videos and games, intersectional representation lags behind, and backlash against 'woke' casting shows resistance. questions.question: Full-Mark Response Evaluate the view that media representations of gender are becoming more progressive. Refer to your CSPs. [15 marks] <div class="
questions.correctAnswer: Media representations of gender have become more progressive in some areas, but change is uneven across media forms and intersecting identities. Progressive representations are increasingly visible. The 'This Girl Can' campaign (BBC, 2017) deliberately challenges the male gaze by representing women as active, powerful, and diverse in body type. It subverts the conventional media language of fitness advertising, which positions women as objects of visual pleasure. Similarly, contemporary TV dramas feature complex female protagonists who drive narrative rather than serving as plot devices for male characters. However, traditional representations persist in other media forms. Music videos continue to objectify women, particularly in hip-hop and pop genres, where female dancers are presented as decorative background. Video games still frequently feature sexualised female character designs and male-dominated protagonist rosters. The 'new man' representation has complicated male representation. While some advertising and TV drama show emotionally articulate, nurturing men, hyper-masculinity remains the dominant representation in action films, video games, and men's lifestyle media. Toxic masculinity is reinforced rather than challenged in many products. Intersectionality reveals further limitations.
